name: Prazosin
lead: Prazosin is a prescription alpha-1 adrenergic receptor blocker, sold since 1976 in the United States as Minipress and now generic. Its US label lists hypertension as its indication [1][2]. In practice it is also prescribed off-label for urinary symptoms of benign prostatic hyperplasia, Raynaud's phenomenon and, most prominently, nightmares associated with post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) [2].

The wiki covers it because of that sleep use. Clinicians who prescribe it for trauma-related nightmares do so to restore uninterrupted sleep, and people who connect sleep with a rested, healthier-looking face see this as an indirect route to looking better. No published trial has tested prazosin for appearance outcomes, and no community threads about it could be cited.
Common adverse effects on the label include dizziness, headache and drowsiness, and the label warns of syncope with sudden loss of consciousness, often linked to postural hypotension [1].

paras: The label lists treatment of hypertension [1]. Wikipedia describes prazosin as a second-line antihypertensive today, and Grokipedia reports that it was studied in hypertension trials from the 1970s onward and was among the first alpha-blockers used for benign prostatic hyperplasia [8][2]. A large Veterans Affairs comparison of six antihypertensive drugs against placebo included prazosin [3], and a 1976 clinical report in the British Medical Journal discussed prazosin in hypertension [9]. An earlier Veterans Administration trial examined vasodilator therapy, including prazosin, in chronic heart failure [4]. A 2024 Medical Letter review of drugs for hypertension places it among the available agents [10].

Wikipedia reports that the psychiatrist Murray Raskind and colleagues noticed in the 1990s that veterans taking prazosin for urinary symptoms reported fewer nightmares, which led to its off-label use for PTSD nightmares. Later meta-analyses reported benefits for sleep and nightmares, whereas a large randomised trial in military veterans with chronic PTSD found no significant benefit over placebo; the 2023 VA/DoD guideline recommends against it for overall PTSD symptoms but weakly in favour of it for nightmares [8].

A 2024 review of trauma-associated sleep disorder, a parasomnia of trauma-related nightmares, disruptive night-time behaviours and autonomic disturbance, describes prazosin as at the forefront of proposed treatment [11]. A 2021 systematic review of PTSD guidelines focused on how they treat nightmares [12], and a 2021 meta-analysis of 115 randomised trials of PTSD drugs reported that SSRIs beat placebo with a small effect size [13].
Wikipedia lists use in severe Indian red scorpion stings, and as possibly useful in heart failure and Raynaud syndrome [8].

Prazosin selectively blocks postsynaptic alpha-1 receptors in vascular smooth muscle, causing vasodilation and lower peripheral resistance [2]. Wikipedia describes it as an inverse agonist at the alpha-1A, alpha-1B and alpha-1D subtypes with far weaker binding at alpha-2 receptors, and says it is thought to cross the blood-brain barrier and dampen noradrenergic arousal, although the mechanism in PTSD is not fully understood [8].
Oral bioavailability is about 60 percent, protein binding about 97 percent, onset 30 to 90 minutes, elimination half-life 2 to 3 hours, and duration of action 10 to 24 hours [8].

The label reports dizziness (10.3 percent), headache (7.8 percent), drowsiness (7.6 percent), lack of energy and weakness among the most frequent reactions, and warns of syncope, including after the first dose [1]. Wikipedia describes a first-dose response of dizziness, drowsiness and low blood pressure on standing, lists less common effects such as nausea, oedema, depression, anxiety and nasal congestion, and notes very rare priapism [8].

Prazosin was developed in Pfizer's medicinal chemistry laboratories and patented in 1965, entered medical use in the 1970s, and was approved by the FDA as Minipress in June 1976. Pfizer's patent expired in May 1989, after which generics appeared [8].

Randomised trials have examined prazosin in alcohol use disorder: a 2018 placebo-controlled study randomised 36 people for six weeks [14], and a 2023 trial in active-duty soldiers analysed predictive effects of cardiovascular parameters [15]. Wikipedia also mentions investigation in insomnia and in cytokine storm, mostly in animal models [8].

Hypertension and heart failure trials involving prazosin were published in 1986 and 1993 [3][4]. Registered trials have examined prazosin for nightmares in PTSD with bulimia and as an add-on in alcohol use disorder in soldiers with and without PTSD [5][6], and the alcohol trials above reported on drinking outcomes [14][15]. A veterans' trial in chronic PTSD found no significant benefit over placebo for overall symptoms [8]. No studies were found testing prazosin for appearance outcomes.

card.summary: A blood-pressure alpha-blocker used off-label for trauma nightmares; nothing connects it to appearance.
card.note: Fainting and low blood pressure, especially after the first dose.

quick.overview:
Prazosin is a prescription alpha-1 blocker approved for high blood pressure. Clinicians also use it off-label for benign prostatic hyperplasia and for nightmares linked to PTSD.

No trial has tested it for looks, and the wiki found no community discussion to cite.
quick.mechanism: It blocks alpha-1 adrenergic receptors, relaxing blood vessels and, for nightmares, dampening noradrenergic activity during sleep according to reference sources.
quick.risks: The label lists dizziness, headache, drowsiness and weakness, and warns of fainting from postural low blood pressure, notably with the first dose. Prescription-only.

chain: Fewer trauma-related nightmares in some patients
More continuous sleep, which people associate with a rested look
angle.text: Prazosin is used medically for trauma-related nightmares and sleep disturbance. People who value sleep for appearance see better sleep as a contributor to a rested face, but this link is theirs and no study has measured looks with prazosin.
